## Introduction
This report replicates key analyses from Ramirez et al., “Carbon pathways and trophic attributes are conserved in carnivorous reef fishes across a major human disturbance gradient,” which investigates how human disturbance influences energy flow and food web structure in a hyperdiverse coral reef ecosystem at Kiritimati Island. The original study leverages advanced stable isotope techniques, including compound-specific amino acid analysis, to evaluate whether shifts in habitat quality and community composition translate into changes in trophic structure and carbon sourcing for reef fishes.

The dataset is based on ecosystem-scale sampling across a well-defined gradient of human disturbance. It includes tissue samples from six carnivorous, generalist reef fish species that collectively represent a large proportion of reef fish biomass. For each sample, both bulk stable isotope values and essential amino acid isotope signatures were measured. These data are paired with isotopic signatures from multiple basal carbon sources, including plankton, detritus, coral-derived material, and epilithic algal matrices, enabling detailed comparison of energy pathways across sites with differing levels of disturbance.

To evaluate trophic structure and energy sourcing, the original study applied a combination of statistical and isotope-based methods. These included bulk isotope analysis to estimate trophic position, compound-specific isotope analysis to resolve carbon sources, and Bayesian mixing models to quantify source contributions. Linear discriminant analysis (LDA) was used to differentiate isotopic fingerprints among sources, while general linear models (GLMs) tested for variation in trophic metrics across the disturbance gradient. Isotopic niche analyses further assessed changes in niche width and position among species.

Despite pronounced differences in reef condition and community composition, the original study found that dominant energy pathways remained largely unchanged. Reef fishes consistently relied on planktonic production and microbially reworked detritus as primary energy sources, with minimal contributions from coral- and algae-based pathways. Trophic positions and niche characteristics were similarly stable across the disturbance gradient. These findings suggest that key energy channels in this system are relatively robust to human disturbance, potentially due to the stabilizing role of generalist consumers and persistent pelagic and detrital inputs.

This replication focuses on reproducing several core components of the original analysis. First, I will calculate and compare summary statistics of relative biomass and abundance, expressed as percentages of the total, across the six fish species and three levels of human disturbance. Second, I will recreate visualizations of essential amino acid isotope values, specifically phenylalanine (Phe) and lysine (Lys), across disturbance levels and sites for each species. Third, I will replicate the inferential component of the study by conducting a linear discriminant analysis (LDA) to evaluate separation among carbon sources based on isotopic signatures. Finally, I will reproduce visualizations of the LDA results to assess how well isotopic fingerprints distinguish among sources and to compare patterns with those reported in the original study.


## Visualization of the Data
Note: Variables can be referenced in the data variable dictionary found at the bottom of the report

ki_bulk_sia.csv is a comma-delimited file containing sample meta-data and bulk stable isotope data for sampled carnivorous reef fish.

ki_csia_c.csv is a comma-delimited file containing sampled meta-data and amino acid-specific stable carbon isotope data for sampled carnivorous reef fish.

ki_csia_n.csv is a comma-delimited file containing sampled meta-data and amino acid-specific stable nitrogen isotope data for sampled carnivorous reef fish.

ki_fish_data_sum.csv is a comma-delimited file containing summary data for fish observed in underwater visual census surveys (from Magel et al. 2020).
```{r}
#load all necessary packages
library(ggplot2)
library(skimr)
library(tidyr)
library(grid)
library(patchwork)
library(reshape2)
library(MASS)
library(ellipse)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyverse)

#Load all data
bulk_sia<- read.csv("data/ki_bulk_sia.csv")
head(bulk_sia) #preview raw data
skim(bulk_sia) #summary statistics

csia_c<- read.csv("data/ki_csia_c.csv")
head(csia_c) #preview raw data
skim(csia_c) #summary statistics

csia_n<- read.csv("data/ki_csia_n.csv")
head(csia_n) #preview raw data
skim(csia_n) #summary statistics

fish_data<- read.csv("data/ki_fish_data_sum.csv")
head(fish_data) #preview raw data
skim(fish_data) #summary statistics
```

## Analysis 1: Summary Statistic Replication
This analysis summarizes and visualizes how fish community structure varies across levels of human disturbance by examining both abundance and biomass across trophic groups. The workflow begins by grouping the dataset by disturbance category and calculating mean total abundance and biomass, along with mean values for each trophic group. These values are then reshaped into long format to facilitate plotting, and converted into relative percentages of the total (i.e., percent contribution of each trophic group to overall abundance or biomass). Factor levels for both disturbance categories and trophic groups are explicitly ordered to match the original study’s presentation.

The processed data are visualized using bar plots that display the percent contribution of each trophic group across disturbance levels, with separate panels (facets) for each category. This approach is applied consistently to both abundance and biomass, allowing for direct comparison between the two metrics. Finally, the abundance and biomass plots are combined into a single figure, replicating the structure of the original analysis and enabling an integrated view of how trophic composition appears across the disturbance gradient.
```{r}
#look at my variables
glimpse(fish_data) 

#Wrangling data for abundance summary statistics
fish_ab <- fish_data %>%
 group_by(dist_cat) %>% 
  summarise(
    total = mean(AB_total, na.rm = TRUE),
    Pi = mean(AB_pisc, na.rm = TRUE),
    GC = mean(AB_gen, na.rm = TRUE),
    De = mean(AB_det, na.rm = TRUE),
    In = mean(AB_inv, na.rm = TRUE),
    Pl = mean(AB_plank, na.rm = TRUE),
    Co = mean(AB_coral, na.rm = TRUE),
    Om = mean(AB_omn, na.rm = TRUE),
    He = mean(AB_herb, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(Pi, GC, De, In, Pl, Co, Om, He),
    names_to = "trophic_group",
    values_to = "AB"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    rel_AB = (AB / total) * 100
  )

#Reordering disturbance categories to match original plot
fish_ab <- fish_ab %>%
  mutate(dist_cat = factor(dist_cat, levels = c("Very Low", "Medium", "Very High")))

#Reordering trophic groups to match original plot
fish_ab <- fish_ab %>%
  mutate(
    trophic_group = factor(
      trophic_group,
      levels = c("De", "He", "Om", "Co", "Pl", "In", "GC", "Pi")))

#Plotting the Total Percent of Fish Abundance by Trophic Group for Each Disturbance Level
fish_ab_plot<- ggplot(fish_ab, aes(x = rel_AB, y = trophic_group,
  fill = dist_cat)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity") +
  facet_wrap(~ dist_cat) +
  labs(y = "Trophic Group", x = "Percent of Total Fish Abundance",
       fill = "Disturbance Level") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = 
        c("Very Low" = "#3A6EA5",
           "Medium" = "#9FD8CB",
          "Very High" = "#9B1D20")) +
  theme_minimal() 
fish_ab_plot

#Wrangling data for biomass summary statistics
fish_bm <- fish_data %>%
  group_by(dist_cat) %>%
  #Calculate means
  summarise(
    total = mean(BM_total, na.rm = TRUE),
    Pi = mean(BM_pisc, na.rm = TRUE),
    GC = mean(BM_gen, na.rm = TRUE),
    De = mean(BM_det, na.rm = TRUE),
    In = mean(BM_inv, na.rm = TRUE),
    Pl = mean(BM_plank, na.rm = TRUE),
    Co = mean(BM_coral, na.rm = TRUE),
    Om = mean(BM_omn, na.rm = TRUE),
    He = mean(BM_herb, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) %>%
  #Reorganizing data for easier plotting
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(Pi, GC, De, In, Pl, Co, Om, He),
    names_to = "trophic_group",
    values_to = "BM"
  ) %>%
  #Calculate percent of total biomass
  mutate(
    rel_BM = (BM / total) * 100
  )

##Reordering disturbance categories to match original plot
fish_bm <- fish_bm %>%
  mutate(dist_cat = factor(dist_cat, levels = c("Very Low", "Medium", "Very High")))

#Reordering trophic groups to match original plot
fish_bm <- fish_bm %>%
  mutate(
    trophic_group = factor(
      trophic_group,
      levels = c("De", "He", "Om", "Co", "Pl", "In", "GC", "Pi")))

#Plotting the Total Percent of Fish Biomass by Trophic Group for Each Disturbance Level
fish_bm_plot<- ggplot(fish_bm, aes(x = rel_BM, y = trophic_group,
  fill = dist_cat)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity") +
  facet_wrap(~ dist_cat) +
  labs(y = "Trophic Group", x = "Percent of Total Fish Biomass",
       fill = "Disturbance Level") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = 
        c("Very Low" = "#3A6EA5",
           "Medium" = "#9FD8CB",
          "Very High" = "#9B1D20")) +
  theme_minimal() 
fish_bm_plot

#Combine plots
fish_sum_plots <- fish_bm_plot/fish_ab_plot
fish_sum_plots #final replication plot of summary statistic analysis

#Comparison of plots
#| out-width: "##%"
knitr::include_graphics("images/Analysis1.png")
fish_sum_plots
```

## Analysis 2: Data Visualization Replication
This analysis focuses on visualizing variation in essential amino acid isotope values (δ¹⁵N) across fish species, disturbance levels, and sampling sites. The dataset is first inspected and prepared by converting species names and disturbance categories into factors with defined ordering to ensure consistency with the original study. Two primary sets of plots are then created for phenylalanine (Phe) and lysine (Lys), showing how isotope values vary across species and disturbance levels. These plots include individual data points along with summary statistics (mean ± standard deviation), allowing for visualization of both variability and central tendencies within each group.

A second set of visualizations examines the same amino acid values across sampling sites rather than disturbance categories. These plots incorporate additional aesthetics (color, fill, and shape) to distinguish among sites and include sample size annotations for each group. Consistent axis scaling and formatting are applied across all plots to facilitate comparison. Finally, all four panels (Phe and Lys by disturbance, and Phe and Lys by site) are combined into a single figure, replicating the structure of the original visualization and providing a comprehensive view of isotopic variation across ecological and spatial gradients.
```{r}

glimpse(csia_n)

#ensure these are considered factors for my plot
csia_n$sci_name <- factor(csia_n$sci_name)
species_order <- rev(levels(csia_n$sci_name))
csia_n$dist_cat <- factor(
  csia_n$dist_cat,
  levels = c("Very Low", "Medium", "Very High"))

#plotting fish species by Phe values across disturbance levels
Phe <- ggplot(csia_n, aes(x = sci_name, y = Phe, fill = dist_cat)) + 
  #raw data
  geom_point(
    shape = 21,
    color = "black",
    size = 2.5,
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.75)
  ) +
  #mean and sd
  stat_summary(
    aes(group = dist_cat, fill = dist_cat),
    fun.data = function(x) {
      dplyr::tibble(
        y = mean(x, na.rm = TRUE),
        ymin = mean(x, na.rm = TRUE) - sd(x, na.rm = TRUE),
        ymax = mean(x, na.rm = TRUE) + sd(x, na.rm = TRUE))}) +
  theme_minimal() +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "Very Low" = "#3A6EA5",
      "Medium" = "#9FD8CB",
      "Very High" = "#9B1D20")) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(1, 10),
    breaks = seq(1, 9, 2)) +
  labs(
    y = "Phenylalanine δ15N Values",
    x = "Species",
    fill = "Disturbance Level") +
  theme(
    legend.position = "top",
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)) +
  scale_x_discrete(limits = rev(levels(csia_n$sci_name))) +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(
      override.aes = list(shape = 21, color = "black")))
Phe

#plotting fish species by Lys values across disturbance levels
Lys <- ggplot(csia_n, aes(x = sci_name, y = Lys, fill = dist_cat)) + 
  #raw data

    shape = 21,
    color = "black",
    size = 2.5,
```

## Analysis 3: Inferential Statistical Analysis Replication
This analysis reproduces the linear discriminant analysis (LDA) used to distinguish among carbon source groups based on essential amino acid isotope signatures. The dataset is first inspected and then subset into two components: a “source” dataset (excluding carnivorous fish groups) used to train the model, and an “animal” dataset containing the carnivorous fish whose source classification is inferred. This separation allows the model to be built exclusively on known source signatures before predicting classifications for consumer organisms.

A linear discriminant analysis is then performed using six amino acids (isoleucine, leucine, lysine, phenylalanine, threonine, and valine) as predictor variables. The model is first run with cross-validation to evaluate classification performance, and a confusion matrix is used to calculate both overall accuracy and group-specific accuracy. A final LDA model is then trained on the full source dataset, and this trained model is used to predict the likely carbon source assignments for carnivorous fish samples.

In addition to prediction, the model output is examined to identify which amino acids contribute most strongly to separation among groups, based on discriminant coefficients. While no direct plots are generated in this replication, the resulting LD1 and LD2 values and classification structure are consistent with those reported in the original study.
```{r}
glimpse(csia_c)

#Subset data
fish.source <- csia_c[!(csia_c$group %in% c("Pi", "GC")), ]
fish.animal <- csia_c[csia_c$group %in% c("Pi", "GC"), ]

#Fit LDA with cross-validation (model + accuracy)
fish.lda <- lda(group ~ Ile + Leu + Lys + Phe + Thr + Val,
                data = fish.source,
                CV = TRUE)

#Evaluate classification accuracy
ct.prod <- table(fish.source$group, fish.lda$class)
overall_accuracy <- sum(diag(prop.table(ct.prod)))
group_accuracy <- diag(prop.table(ct.prod, 1))

#Train final model
fish.train <- lda(group ~ Ile + Leu + Lys + Phe + Thr + Val,
                  data = fish.source)

#Predict carbon sources for carnivorous fish
animal.res <- predict(fish.train, fish.animal)

# coefficients (which amino acids matter)
fish.train 

#Comparison: no plots, however LD1 and LD2 values match what is reported in the paper
```

## Analysis 4: Data Visualization Plot Replication
This analysis reconstructs and visualizes the linear discriminant analysis (LDA) results used to separate carbon sources and predict dietary contributions for carnivorous reef fishes based on essential amino acid isotope signatures. The process begins by extracting LDA coordinates for the source dataset and combining them with metadata such as fish code, species identity, and disturbance category. The trained LDA model is then applied to the carnivorous fish dataset to generate predicted group assignments, posterior probabilities, and discriminant scores, which are also formatted into a structured dataset for visualization.

To enable comparison between groups, both source and consumer datasets are merged into a single dataframe containing LD1 and LD2 scores. The data are then reorganized to match the species ordering used in the original study, and LD2 values are flipped to ensure alignment with the published orientation of the ordination space. In addition, confidence ellipses are generated for each carbon source group based on covariance structure, providing a visual representation of group dispersion in discriminant space.

The final visualization combines multiple components: carbon source ellipses outlining group separation, source points representing baseline isotope signatures, and fish points colored by species to show predicted dietary associations. This integrated LDA plot allows direct comparison of source clustering and consumer positioning within isotopic space. Overall, the replicated figure closely mirrors the original LDA visualization, capturing similar patterns of separation among carbon sources and consistent placement of consumer species within the graph.
```{r}
#Create data sets with these LDA coordinates
datPred <- data.frame(fish_code = fish.source$fish_code, group=fish.source$group, sci_name = fish.source$sci_name, dist_cat = fish.source$dist_cat, predict(fish.train)$x) 

#Predict the carnivorous fish fractions based on ESS
animal.res <- predict(fish.train, fish.animal)
class <- cbind(animal.res$class, animal.res$posterior, animal.res$x)

#Save the predicted coordinates 
datPred2 <- data.frame(fish_code = fish.animal$fish_code, dist_cat = fish.animal$dist_cat, sci_name = fish.animal$sci_name, group='Pi',
                       animal.res$x)

#Merge the source and animal dataframes for plotting
datPred3 <- rbind(datPred , datPred2)
colnames(datPred3)[1] <- "fish_code"

dat_ell <- data.frame() 

datPred$group <- as.factor(datPred$group)
datPred$group <- factor(datPred$group, level = c("Co", "De", "He", "Zp"))

for(g in levels(datPred$group)){ 
  dat_ell <- rbind(dat_ell, cbind(as.data.frame(with(datPred[datPred$group==g,], 
                                                     ellipse(cor(LD1, LD2), 
                                                             scale=c(sd(LD1), sd(LD2)), 
                                                             centre=c(mean(LD1), mean(LD2))))), group=g)) } 

#levels(datPred3$sci_name)
datPred3$sci_name <- factor(datPred3$sci_name, level = c("Chaetodon ornatissimus","Ctenochaetus marginatus","Acanthurus nigricans","Pseudanthias olivaceus",
                                                 "Aphareus furca", "Caranx melampygus","Cephalopholis argus",  "Lutjanus bohar", "Cephalopholis urodeta", "Lutjanus fulvus"))

#flip so axes match the original plot
datPred3$LD2 <- -datPred3$LD2
dat_ell$y <- -dat_ell$y

#Create subsets
fish_points <- datPred3[datPred3$group %in% c("Pi", "GC"), ]        # carnivorous fish
source_points <- datPred3[!(datPred3$group %in% c("Pi", "GC")), ]   # carbon sources
ellipses <- dat_ell[!(dat_ell$group %in% c("Pi", "GC")), ]          # ellipses for sources 

#Create plot
lda_plot<- ggplot(datPred3, aes(x = LD1, y = LD2, shape = group)) +
  #carbon source ellipses
  geom_path(data = ellipses,
            aes(x = x, y = y),
            linetype = 2,
            size = 0.75) +
  #carbon source points
  geom_point(data = source_points,
             size = 4) +
  # fish points 
  geom_point(data = fish_points,
             aes(color = sci_name),
             size = 5,
             alpha = 0.85) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(0, 2, 5, 19, 6)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#6699CC", "#7D70BA", "#CFFFB0",
                                "#F3D34A", "#FF8C42", "#A23E48")) +
  labs(x = expression(LD[1]~"(83.47%)"),
       y = expression(LD[2]~"(13.92%)"),
       color = "Species",
       shape = "Carbon Source") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text = element_text(color = "black"),
    text = element_text(size = 14),
    axis.ticks.length = unit(2.5, "mm"),
    legend.position = "top",
    plot.title.position = "plot") 
lda_plot

#Compare plots
#| out-width: "##%"
knitr::include_graphics("images/Analysis4.jpeg")
lda_plot 
```

## Disscussion & Reflection
Overall, the replication of analyses from Ramirez et al. was largely successful. The majority of summary statistics, visualizations, and inferential results closely matched those presented in the original paper, indicating that the main patterns and conclusions are reproducible using the provided data. In particular, comparisons of relative biomass and abundance across disturbance levels, as well as visualizations of essential amino acid values, were consistent with the published results. The linear discriminant analysis (LDA) and its associated plots also showed similar separation among carbon sources, suggesting that the key structure of the data was effectively reproduced.

While the replication was largely successful, there were some challenges encountered throughout the process. At times, it was not entirely clear how certain variables were processed or how specific figures were generated in the original study. This made it difficult to determine whether discrepancies were due to coding differences or underlying data handling steps that were not explicitly described. In a few cases, brief reference to the original code helped clarify these issues, but the majority of the replication was completed independently. These challenges highlight the importance of clear methodological descriptions and detailed reporting of data processing steps in published studies.

Some minor differences between the replicated results and the original outputs likely stem from differences in coding approaches and implementation. My analyses relied heavily on packages such as dplyr for data manipulation and summarization, whereas the original study primarily used base R functions. Although both approaches are valid, small differences in grouping behavior, ordering of factors, or handling of missing values can lead to slight variations in results or figure appearance. Despite these minor inconsistencies, the overall agreement between the replicated and original analyses suggests that the results are robust and that the study’s conclusions are well supported.

## References:
Ramirez MD, McMahon KW, Rooney N, El-Sabaawi RW, Baum JK. 2026. Carbon pathways and trophic attributes are conserved in carnivorous reef fishes across a major human disturbance gradient. Journal of Animal Ecology 95: 39–53. 

## Data Dictionary:
Data set: ki_bulk_sia.csv
Variables:

  * id: alphanumeric unique identification code for an individual
  * species: identification code for species 
  * sci_name: scientific name
  * group: fish trophic group (Pi = piscivore, GC = generalist carnivore)
  * year: calendar year of sample collection
  * site: identification code for sampling location
  * dist_cat: local human disturbance level category (see manuscript for details)
  * weight_.g.: fish weight in grams
  * total_length_.mm.: total fish length in millimeters
  * standard_length_.mm.: standard fish length in millimeters
  * d13C (‰): bulk stable carbon isotope values; permil
  * d15N (‰): bulk stable nitrogen isotope value; permil
  * C.N: ratio of percent carbon to percent nitrogen in bulk SIA sample
  
Data set: ki_csia_c.csv
Variables:

  * fish_code: condensed alphanumeric unique identification code for an individual
  * species_code: condensed identification code for species 
  * id: alphanumeric unique identification code for an individual
  * sci_name: scientific name
  * group: fish trophic group (Pi = piscivore, GC = generalist carnivore, He = herbivore, De = detritivore, Co = corallivore, Zp = zooplanktivore)
  * site: identification code for sampling location
  * dist_cat: local human disturbance level category (see manuscript for details)
  * isotope: stable isotope measured
  * n_inj: number of sample injections on GC-C-IRMS per sample
  * Columns 10 through 37: amino acid-specific stable carbon isotope values for sampled fish. Three letter codes denote each amino acid: Ala = alanine, Gly = glycine, Thr = threonine, Ser = serine, Val = valine, Leu = leucine, Ile = isoleucine, Pro = proline, Asp = aspartic acid, Glu = glutamic acid, Phe = phenylalanine, Lys = lysine. Values are means of triplicate injections. Columns with the suffix "SD" denote the standard deviation of the triplicate injections for each isotope and amino acid.

Data set: ki_csia_n.csv
Variables:

 * fish_code: condensed alphanumeric unique identification code for an individual
  * species_code: condensed identification code for species 
  * id: alphanumeric unique identification code for an individual
  * sci_name: scientific name
  * group: fish trophic group (Pi = piscivore, GC = generalist carnivore, He = herbivore, De = detritivore, Co =     corallivore, Zp = zooplanktivore)
  * site: identification code for sampling location
  * dist_cat: local human disturbance level category (see manuscript for details)
  * pub.name: alternative site name
  * continous.pressure.2km: quantitative human pressure value (see manuscript for details)
  * wgt_g: fish weight in grams
  * tot_len_mm: total fish length in millimeters
  * std_len_mm: standard fish length in millimeters
  * isotope: stable isotope measured
  * n_inj: number of sample injections on GC-C-IRMS per sample
  * sumV = microbial resynthesis 
  * Columns 15 through 46: amino acid-specific stable nitrogen isotope values for sampled fish. Three letter codes denote each amino acid: Ala = alanine, Gly = glycine, Thr = threonine, Ser = serine, Val = valine, Leu = leucine, Ile = isoleucine, Pro = proline, Asp = aspartic acid, Glu = glutamic acid, Phe = phenylalanine, Lys = lysine. Values are means of triplicate injections. Columns with the suffix "SD" denote the standard deviation of the triplicate injections for each isotope and amino acid.

Data set: ki_fish_data_sum.csv
Variables:

* year: calendar year of sample collection
  * date: date in day_month_year format
  * site: identification code for sampling location
  * observer: initials of the observer who conducted the survey
  * dist_cat: local human disturbance level category (see manuscript for details)
  * Columns 6 through 23: biomass (BM) and abundance (AB) estimates for all fish (total) and by trophic group (corallivores = 'coral', detritivores = 'det', generalist carnivores = 'gen', herbivores = 'herb', invertivores = 'inv', omnivores = 'omn', piscivores = 'pisc', planktivores = 'plank')
